headline: Genetic Proof Traces Smallpox’s Arrival in the Americas to European Colonizers
deck: Ancient DNA from Chilean mummies confirms that smallpox was introduced to the hemisphere by European invaders, ending centuries of debate over the pandemic’s origins.
body: Laboratory analysis of genetic material extracted from 16th-century Chilean mummies has delivered the first conclusive proof that smallpox crossed the Atlantic with European colonizers. The study, published this week, marks the first time researchers have sequenced ancient smallpox genomes directly from human remains in the Americas, closing a historical void that has long obscured the pandemic’s true introduction point. The findings dismantle competing theories that the virus arrived earlier through unknown routes and instead place the blame squarely on the ships, soldiers, and settlers who landed in the 1500s. For historians and epidemiologists alike, the discovery is a turning point—one that rewrites the early chronicle of disease transfer during conquest.

Researchers isolated viral DNA from the preserved tissues of Inca mummies exhumed in northern Chile, confirming that the strain carried genetic markers indistinguishable from European variants circulating in the same era. The match is exact enough to exclude any independent evolution within the Americas, leaving little room for alternative explanations. Senior author Dr. Lars Hansen of the University of Copenhagen said the data provides ‘clear evidence’ that colonization brought smallpox to these shores. ‘We can now say with genetic certainty that the virus Europeans carried caused the first recorded epidemics in the Inca heartland,’ Hansen told reporters.

The breakthrough emerged from a painstaking extraction process that yielded fragments of variola major DNA despite centuries of degradation. Unlike modern smallpox samples, which are well documented, historical strains from the Americas have been notoriously difficult to recover. Yet the team’s success—based on samples drawn from skeletal and soft-tissue remains—demonstrates that ancient pathogens can survive in unexpected repositories when conditions are right. Sites in the Atacama Desert, with their arid climate and naturally mummifying conditions, proved ideal for preservation.

Beyond confirming transmission vectors, the study offers a surprising reassessment of smallpox lethality in the pre-modern era. Genetic markers associated with immune evasion and host adaptation suggest that the historical strain may have been less virulent than later 18th- and 19th-century variants. This nuance complicates the assumption that all early smallpox outbreaks were uniformly catastrophic, forcing scholars to reconsider how mortality rates varied across time and geography. ‘We may have overestimated the deadliness of the first wave,’ noted evolutionary biologist Dr. Elena Rojas in a commentary accompanying the paper.

Historical records have long implicated smallpox in the staggering Indigenous population collapse that followed European arrival, but direct biological evidence has been scarce. The new data bridges that gap, offering a genetic Rosetta Stone for understanding how Old World pathogens reshaped entire civilizations. Analysts now argue that the pandemic’s scale was not merely the result of immunological naivety but also of deliberate transmission tactics—warfare, forced migration, and contaminated trade routes—that accelerated viral spread.

The study’s geographic focus on Chile’s northern coast underscores a critical but often overlooked corridor of contact between Europeans and Indigenous groups. While Mexico and the Caribbean have received more attention for early epidemics, the Atacama region—home to the Inca empire’s southern periphery—emerges as a key transmission zone. Researchers suggest that Inca populations, already weakened by conflict and famine, were further debilitated by sequential smallpox outbreaks that arrived via Spanish expeditions probing the continent’s interior.

Critics caution that even definitive genetic evidence cannot fully reconstruct the human toll, which remains buried in unmarked graves and erased from colonial archives. Yet the findings carry immediate implications for how future pandemics are studied, demonstrating that ancient DNA can serve as a silent witness to historical injustice. As global health experts grapple with emerging pathogens, the study serves as a stark reminder that colonization’s epidemiological legacy endures long after the last gunshot fades.

The research team has called for broader genomic surveys across North and South America to map the full footprint of smallpox’s arrival. Such work could reveal whether multiple introductions occurred or if a single strain seeded cascading outbreaks. For descendant Indigenous communities, the findings validate oral histories that have long linked disease surges to the violence of conquest. ‘Our ancestors knew the truth,’ said a representative of the Aymara people in a statement to AP News. ‘Now science has caught up with memory.’
